findings.title: New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider added abstract method int order() with no default implementation. Any out-of-tree custom CryptoProvider compiled against the old interface will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorts by CryptoProvider::order, and will fail to compile against the new interface. As a public SPI this is a binary and source incompatible change. It should be a default method returning a sensible default.

findings.title: Equal-order providers selected nondeterministically, losing fail-fast
findings.body: Previously multiple CryptoProviders on the classpath threw IllegalStateException. Now providers are sorted by order() reversed and the first is silently used, with others only logged at debug. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so if any two are present the winner depends on ServiceLoader iteration order which is classpath order dependent. This can silently swap FIPS for non-FIPS or vice versa with no warning, violating compliance expectations and hiding misconfiguration.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns default KeyStore provider instead of BouncyCastle
findings.body: The method contract is to return the BouncyCastle security provider, but the implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which on a standard JDK is SUN or SunJSSE, not BouncyCastle. Callers expecting BouncyCastle-specific behavior will get the wrong provider. WildFlyElytronProvider returns null when there is no BouncyCastle provider; this implementation should do the same or throw UnsupportedOperationException instead of returning a misleading provider.

findings.title: ECDSA integer conversion silently truncates oversized and negative values
findings.body: asn1derToConcatenatedRS decodes r/s with new BigInteger(bytes) which accepts negative integers, then integerToBytes truncates to qLength by copying the last qLength bytes without checking the dropped bytes. A DER value larger than the curve size or negative will be silently truncated to a different valid-looking value instead of throwing IOException. This masks invalid signatures, accepts non-canonical encodings, and can cause incorrect verification decisions. Dropped bytes must be verified to be zero and negatives rejected.

findings.title: readSequence does not enforce exact length and ignores trailing data
findings.body: readSequence loops while length > 0 subtracting each element size but never checks that length ends at exactly zero and never checks that no bytes remain after the sequence. An inner element that overruns the declared outer length makes length negative and the loop exits successfully, and trailing garbage after the sequence is ignored. DER signature parsing must be strict and reject overlong, short, or trailing-data encodings to avoid malleability.

findings.title: concatenatedRSToASN1DER lacks length validation and throws AIOOBE
findings.body: The method assumes the input signature length equals signLength and immediately does System.arraycopy with len = signLength/2 without validation. A caller passing a truncated, overlong, or odd signLength gets ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of the declared IOException, and odd lengths are silently mishandled by integer division. It should validate signature != null, signature.length == signLength, and signLength even, and throw IOException otherwise.

findings.title: Test reuses P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and never verifies signature
findings.body: The test generates one EC key pair with the default curve, typically P-256, and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512 while only varying the target concatenated length. For ES384 and ES512 the conversion just zero-pads, so the round-trip assert passes without exercising real P-384 or P-521 sizes. It also only checks round-trip equality and never calls Signature.verify on the re-encoded DER, so a conversion that produces cryptographically invalid DER would still pass.
